items.title: Origin of the Kushanas — the Yue-Chi
items.body:
## Origin of the Kushanas — the Yue-Chi

**In one line:** The Kushanas were a Central Asian people, one branch of the Yue-Chi (Yuezhi), who built a great empire linking Central Asia with northern India.

**Why it is asked:** The *parent stock* (Yuezhi) and the *regions they first held* are standard one-markers. Define once: *Yue-Chi (Yuezhi)* = a Central Asian tribal confederation; *Gandhara* = the region around Peshawar/Taxila; *Indus Basin* = the plains along the Indus river.

**The story (cause → event → result):**
- **Cause:** steppe conflicts pushed the Yuezhi westward from China's frontier.
- **Event:** one branch, the **Kushanas**, moved into **Gandhara, the Kabul Valley and the Indus Basin**; **Kujula Kadphises I** then united the Yue-Chi tribes.
- **Result:** a new empire formed that reshaped Indian **politics, religion, economy and art**.

**Terms explained:** *confederation* = a loose union of tribes; *dominance* = holding firm control over a region.

**Don't confuse:** the **Kushanas** were a branch of the **Yuezhi**, the very people who had earlier *displaced the Shakas* — so the Yuezhi/Kushanas end up pushing out the Shakas in India.

**Remember it:** "**Kushanas = a Yue-Chi branch; Kujula unites them.**"

**TL;DR**
- Kushanas = a Central Asian tribe from the Yue-Chi (Yuezhi).
- First held Gandhara, the Kabul Valley and the Indus Basin.
- Kujula Kadphises I united the Yue-Chi and founded the empire.
- Their rule brought major cultural, religious, economic and artistic change.
keyPoints: Kushanas = a Central Asian tribe from the Yue-Chi (Yuezhi) Confederation.
Established dominance over Gandhara, the Kabul Valley and the Indus Basin.
Expanded the empire into both India and Central Asia.
Kujula Kadphises (I) united the Yue-Chi tribes and founded the empire.
Their rule brought major cultural, religious, economic and artistic change.
items.mnemonic: Roots — 'Kushanas came from the Yue-Chi', Central Asia to the Indus.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (overview; Key Rulers)

items.title: The Kadphises Kings — Foundation & Gold Coins
items.body:
## The Kadphises Kings — Foundation & Gold Coins

**In one line:** The two Kadphises kings built the Kushana state — Kujula founded it, and Vima expanded it and minted abundant gold.

**Why it is asked:** The "who did what" split between the two Kadphises rulers is a frequent match item. Define once: *Roman-inspired coins* = coins modelled on the weight/standard of Roman money; *Shaivite* = a worshipper of Shiva.

**The story:**
- **Kujula Kadphises I (15–64 CE):** united the Yue-Chi tribes, **established the empire**, and issued **Roman-inspired gold coins**.
- **Vima Kadphises II (64–78 CE):** **expanded to Mathura and the Indus basin**, issued **large quantities of gold coins**, and was a **devotee of Shiva** (his coins show Shiva and the bull Nandi).

Together they laid the base that **Kanishka I** would later carry to its height.

**Picture it:**

| Ruler | Reign | Did what |
|---|---|---|
| Kujula Kadphises I | 15–64 CE | United the Yue-Chi; founded the empire; Roman-style gold coins |
| Vima Kadphises II | 64–78 CE | Expanded to Mathura/Indus; abundant gold coins; Shiva devotee |

**Terms explained:** *Nandi* = Shiva's bull mount, a Shaiva symbol seen on Vima's coins.

**Don't confuse:** **Kujula = founder**; **Vima = expander and gold-coin / Shiva king**. Do not swap their roles.

**Remember it:** "**Kujula founds, Vima expands (to Mathura) and mints gold.**"

**TL;DR**
- Kujula Kadphises I (15–64 CE): founded the empire; Roman-inspired gold coins.
- Vima Kadphises II (64–78 CE): expanded to Mathura and the Indus basin.
- Vima issued large quantities of gold coins and worshipped Shiva.
- They set the stage for Kanishka I.
keyPoints: Kujula Kadphises I (15–64 CE): founded the empire; issued Roman-inspired gold coins.
Vima Kadphises II (64–78 CE): expanded to Mathura and the Indus basin.
Vima Kadphises II issued large quantities of gold coins.
Vima Kadphises II was a devotee of Shiva.
The Kadphises kings set the base for Kanishka I's expansion.
items.mnemonic: Two Kadphises — 'Kujula founds, Vima expands (to Mathura) & mints gold'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Key Rulers of the Kushana Empire)

items.title: Kanishka I — The Greatest Kushana
items.body:
## Kanishka I — The Greatest Kushana

**In one line:** Kanishka I was the greatest Kushana ruler, whose 78 CE accession marks the start of the Saka era and whose empire ran from Central Asia deep into the Ganges valley.

**Why it is asked:** The **78 CE / Saka era** link, the **twin capitals**, and the **Devputra** title are repeat questions. Define once: *accession* = coming to the throne; *era* = a year-counting system from a fixed starting event.

**The story (cause → event → result):**
- **Cause:** the Kadphises kings had already built a strong base.
- **Event:** Kanishka (78–105 CE) extended rule from **Central Asia to the Ganges valley** and **Khorasan to Varanasi**, governing from twin capitals at **Purushapura (Peshawar)** and **Mathura**; he patronised **Mahayana Buddhism** and built stupas and monasteries.
- **Result:** his accession year, **78 CE**, became the base of the **Saka era** (India's national calendar), and he proclaimed sacred kingship through the title **"Devputra" (Son of God)**.

**Terms explained:** *Purushapura* = ancient Peshawar; *Khorasan* = a region of eastern Iran/Afghanistan; *Devputra* = "Son of God".

**Don't confuse:** Kanishka's **Saka era = 78 CE**, *not* the Vikram Samvat (58 BCE).

**Remember it:** "**Kanishka '78' — Saka era; Purushapura + Mathura; Devputra.**"

**TL;DR**
- Kanishka I reigned 78–105 CE; 78 CE starts the Saka era (he is credited as founder).
- Empire from Central Asia to the Ganges valley, Khorasan to Varanasi.
- Twin capitals: Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura.
- Patron of Mahayana Buddhism; title 'Devputra' (Son of God).

figure.alt: Map of the Kushan Empire showing Purushapura (Peshawar), Gandhara, Mathura and trade routes to the Ganges valley
figure.caption: The Kushan Empire under Kanishka I — stretching from Central Asia to the Ganges valley, with capitals at Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura, straddling the Silk Route.

keyPoints: Kanishka I reigned 78–105 CE; 78 CE marks the start of the Saka era (credited as founder).
Empire ran from Central Asia to the Ganges valley, Khorasan to Varanasi.
Ruled from twin capitals: Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura.
Made Mahayana Buddhism prominent; built stupas and monasteries.
Adopted the divine title 'Devputra' (Son of God).
items.mnemonic: Kanishka '78' — Saka era begins; capitals 'Purushapura + Mathura'; title 'Devputra'.

items.title: Fourth Buddhist Council & the Rise of Mahayana
items.body:
## Fourth Buddhist Council & the Rise of Mahayana

**In one line:** Kanishka called the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir, where Buddhism formally split into Mahayana and Hinayana and Mahayana began spreading abroad.

**Why it is asked:** Patron, venue and president of each Buddhist council are classic match questions. Define once: *Mahayana* ("Great Vehicle") = the devotional, Buddha-as-divine form of Buddhism; *Hinayana* ("Lesser Vehicle") = the older, monastic form.

**The story (cause → event → result):**
- **Cause:** doctrinal differences among Buddhist schools needed settling.
- **Event:** Kanishka convened the **Fourth Buddhist Council** in **Srinagar, Kashmir** (at Kundalavana), **presided over by Vasumitra**, with **Ashvaghosha** as a leading scholar.
- **Result:** the council marked the **Mahayana–Hinayana division**, and under Kanishka's patronage **Mahayana Buddhism spread to China and Central Asia** along the Silk Route.

**Picture it — the four councils:**

| Council | Patron | Venue |
|---|---|---|
| First | Ajatashatru | Rajagriha |
| Second | Kalasoka | Vaishali |
| Third | Ashoka | Pataliputra |
| Fourth | Kanishka | Kashmir (Kundalavana) |

**Terms explained:** *council* = a gathering of monks to fix doctrine and texts; *Vasumitra* = the president of the Fourth Council.

**Don't confuse:** the **Fourth Council (Kanishka, Kashmir)** is different from the **Third (Ashoka, Pataliputra)**; the president was **Vasumitra**, not Nagasena (who debated the Indo-Greek king Menander).

**Remember it:** "**4th Council = Kashmir + Kanishka + Vasumitra → Mahayana/Hinayana split.**"

**TL;DR**
- Kanishka convened the Fourth Buddhist Council at Srinagar (Kundalavana), Kashmir.
- President Vasumitra; Ashvaghosha a leading scholar.
- Marked the Mahayana–Hinayana split.
- Mahayana Buddhism spread to China and Central Asia.

figure.alt: Gandhara-school seated Buddha carved in grey stone with Hellenistic drapery
figure.caption: Mahayana Buddhism gained ground under Kanishka; the era's Gandhara art gave the Buddha a Graeco-Roman form.

keyPoints: Kanishka convened the Fourth Buddhist Council at Srinagar, Kashmir.
Presided over by Vasumitra; Ashvaghosha associated as a leading scholar.
Marked the split between Mahayana and Hinayana Buddhism.
Mahayana Buddhism flourished and spread to China and Central Asia.
items.mnemonic: 4th Council = 'Kashmir + Kanishka + Vasumitra' → Mahayana vs Hinayana split.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Kanishka I: Fourth Buddhist Council; Religion and Society)

items.title: Schools of Art — Gandhara, Mathura & Amravati
items.body:
## Schools of Art — Gandhara, Mathura & Amravati

**In one line:** The Kushana age produced three great sculpture schools — Gandhara and Mathura (both Kushana-patronised) and Amravati in the south — each with its own material and style.

**Why it is asked:** Material-and-style matching (which school used which stone) is the top art question. Define once: *Hellenistic* = Greek-influenced; *schist* = the blue-grey stone of Gandhara; *Jataka tales* = stories of the Buddha's past lives.

**The story:** As Buddhism and wealth grew, sculpture flourished. The **Kushanas** backed the **Gandhara** and **Mathura** schools; the southern **Amravati** school rose under the **Satavahanas and Ikshvakus**.

**Picture it:**

| Feature | Gandhara | Mathura | Amravati |
|---|---|---|---|
| Theme | Mainly Buddhist | Hindu, Buddhist & Jain | Jataka tales & Buddha's life |
| Style | Realistic, Hellenistic | Indigenous, bold, muscular | Narrative, intricate reliefs |
| Material | Blue-grey stone (schist) | Red sandstone | White marble-like stone |
| Patrons | Kushanas | Kushanas | Satavahanas, Ikshvakus |
| Centres | Gandhara, Bamyan | Mathura, Kankalitila | Amravati, Nagarjunakonda |

**Terms explained:** *drapery* = the carved folds of cloth; the Gandhara Buddha wears Greek-style drapery with wavy hair.

**Don't confuse:** **Gandhara = grey schist, Greek look**; **Mathura = red sandstone, indigenous**; **Amravati = white marble-like, southern (NOT Kushana) patrons**.

**Remember it:** "**Gandhara = Grey & Greek; Mathura = Maroon (red) & Muscular; Amravati = white Marble & narrative.**"

**TL;DR**
- Kushanas patronised the Gandhara and Mathura schools.
- Gandhara: blue-grey schist, Hellenistic Buddha with Greek drapery.
- Mathura: red sandstone, indigenous robust figures.
- Amravati: white marble-like stone, Jataka reliefs; patrons Satavahanas/Ikshvakus.

figure.alt: Mathura-school seated Buddha carved in red sandstone with robust Indian features
figure.caption: Mathura School: robust, indigenous figures in red sandstone — contrasting with the Hellenistic grey-stone Gandhara Buddha.

keyPoints: Kushanas patronised the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.
Gandhara: blue-grey stone, Hellenistic Buddha with Greek drapery and wavy hair.
Mathura: red sandstone, indigenous robust figures with Indian motifs.
Amravati (Satavahana/Ikshvaku patrons): white marble-like stone, narrative Jataka reliefs.
Locations — Gandhara/Bamyan, Mathura/Kankalitila, Amravati/Nagarjunakonda.
items.mnemonic: Art schools — 'Gandhara = Grey & Greek, Mathura = Maroon (red) & Muscular, Amravati = white Marble & narrative'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Three Schools of Art)

items.title: Court Scholars & Literary–Scientific Contributions
items.body:
## Court Scholars & Literary–Scientific Contributions

**In one line:** Kanishka's court was a hub of Sanskrit learning, hosting the poet Ashvaghosha, the physician Charaka, the philosopher Nagarjuna and (in this period) Vatsyayana.

**Why it is asked:** Scholar-to-work matching is a reliable question, and Nagarjuna is a common "forgotten" name. Define once: *Ayurveda* = the Indian system of medicine; *Mahayana philosophy* = the thought behind the "Great Vehicle" school.

**The story:** Wealth and Buddhist patronage drew scholars to the Kushana court. Their works span poetry, medicine, philosophy and social custom, and Greek contact even added **astronomical/astrological** terms such as *horoscope*.

**Picture it:**

| Scholar | Known for |
|---|---|
| Ashvaghosha | Buddhacharita (life of the Buddha); Saundarananda |
| Charaka | Charaka Samhita — "father of Ayurveda" |
| Nagarjuna | Madhyamika / Sunyavada (Doctrine of the Void) |
| Vatsyayana | Kamasutra |

**Terms explained:** *Buddhacharita* = a Sanskrit biography of the Buddha; *Sunyavada* = the "doctrine of emptiness/void" in Mahayana thought.

**Don't confuse:** **Charaka = medicine (Ayurveda)**; **Nagarjuna = philosophy (Sunyavada)** — do not swap them.

**Remember it:** mnemonic **"A-C-N-V"** — **A**shvaghosha, **C**haraka, **N**agarjuna, **V**atsyayana.

**TL;DR**
- Ashvaghosha wrote the Buddhacharita.
- Charaka, father of Ayurveda, was patronised by Kanishka.
- Nagarjuna founded the Madhyamika/Sunyavada school.
- Vatsyayana composed the Kamasutra; Greek contact added terms like 'horoscope'.
keyPoints: Ashvaghosha wrote the Buddhacharita, a biography of the Buddha.
Charaka, father of Ayurveda, was patronised by Kanishka.
Vatsyayana composed the Kamasutra in this period.
Greek influence introduced astronomical/astrological terms like 'horoscope'.
The court was a centre of Sanskrit literature, medicine and science.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Scientific and Literary Contributions)

items.title: Administration — Satraps & Dual Rule
items.body:
## Administration — Satraps & Dual Rule

**In one line:** The Kushanas ran their huge empire through a tiered system — provinces under chief satraps, districts and villages below — plus a distinctive dual-rule arrangement.

**Why it is asked:** The province → district → village officer ladder is a match item. Define once: *Mahakshatrapa* = chief satrap (military governor of a province); *dual rule* = two kings sharing power at the same time.

**The story:** To hold distant lands, the empire was split into **satrapies (provinces)**, each under a **Mahakshatrapa** who was *both administrator and military commander*. Below him, **districts** were run by the semi-military **Dandanayaka / Mahadandanayaka**, and **villages** by headmen — the **Gramika / Padrapala** — handling **tax and law and order**. The Kushanas also used **dual hereditary rule** (two rulers concurrently) for stability, and their satraps guarded the **Silk Route**.

**Picture it — the ladder:**

| Level | Officer |
|---|---|
| Province (satrapy) | Mahakshatrapa (chief satrap) |
| District | Dandanayaka / Mahadandanayaka |
| Village | Gramika / Padrapala |

**Terms explained:** *Dandanayaka* = a district-level semi-military official; *Gramika* = a village headman.

**Don't confuse:** the **Mahakshatrapa** governs a *province*, not a village; the village head is the **Gramika**.

**Remember it:** "**Mahakshatrapa → Dandanayaka → Gramika**" (province → district → village).

**TL;DR**
- Provinces (satrapies) under a Mahakshatrapa (chief military governor).
- Districts under Dandanayaka / Mahadandanayaka.
- Villages under Gramika / Padrapala — tax and law & order.
- Dual hereditary rule for stability; satraps guarded the Silk Route.
keyPoints: Provinces = Satrapies, each under a Mahakshatrapa (chief military governor).
Districts run by Dandanayaka / Mahadandanayaka (semi-military officials).
Villages run by Gramika / Padrapala (headmen) — tax collection and law & order.
Dual hereditary rule: two rulers shared power concurrently for stability.
Satraps defended trade routes along the Silk Route.
items.mnemonic: Ladder of rule — 'Mahakshatrapa → Dandanayaka → Gramika' (province → district → village).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Administration of the Kushana Empire)

items.title: Coinage, Economy & the Silk Route
items.body:
## Coinage, Economy & the Silk Route

**In one line:** The Kushanas grew rich by controlling the Silk Route and backed it with abundant gold, silver and copper coins on the Roman standard.

**Why it is asked:** The three metals, the multi-faith deities, the Roman standard and the Silk Route trade are all tested. Define once: *Silk Route* = the overland trade network linking China, India and Rome; *toll* = a fee charged for using a trade route.

**The story (cause → event → result):**
- **Cause:** the empire straddled the great east–west trade roads.
- **Event:** the Kushanas issued **gold, silver and copper coins** (gold for trade bearing **Shiva, Buddha and Zeus**; silver for regional trade with ruler portraits; copper for daily use), adopted **Roman coin standards**, and controlled the **Silk Route**.
- **Result:** flourishing **Indo-Roman trade** and **toll revenue**; they *imported* silk and spices and *exported* gold, precious stones and ivory, while **irrigation in Afghanistan and Pakistan** boosted farming.

**Picture it:**

| Metal | Use | Icons |
|---|---|---|
| Gold | Long-distance trade | Shiva, Buddha, Zeus |
| Silver | Regional trade | Kushana ruler portraits |
| Copper | Daily use | Temples, local symbols |

**Terms explained:** *Indo-Roman trade* = commerce between India and the Roman world; *Roman standard* = Roman coin weights/measures.

**Don't confuse:** the Kushanas were famous for **abundant coinage**, so any claim that they "abandoned coins for barter" is false.

**Remember it:** "**Gold, Silver, Copper on the Roman standard — wealth from the Silk Route.**"

**TL;DR**
- Issued gold, silver and copper coins in large quantities.
- Gold coins showed Shiva, Buddha and Zeus; adopted Roman standards.
- Controlled the Silk Route — Indo-Roman trade plus toll revenue.
- Imported silk and spices; exported gold, gems and ivory; irrigation aided farming.
keyPoints: Issued gold, silver and copper coins in large quantities.
Gold coins featured Shiva, Buddha and Greek gods like Zeus; adopted Roman standards.
Controlled the Silk Route — Indo-Roman trade plus toll revenue.
Promoted agriculture with irrigation in Afghanistan and Pakistan.
Imported silk & spices; exported gold, precious stones and ivory.
items.mnemonic: Coins G-S-C — 'Gold (trade), Silver (regional), Copper (daily)'; wealth from the Silk Route.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Coinage and Economy of the Kushanas)

items.title: Religion & Society — Pluralism under the Kushanas
items.body:
## Religion & Society — Pluralism under the Kushanas

**In one line:** Kushana society was strikingly plural — Mahayana Buddhism flourished, kings worshipped Shiva, and coins carried many gods, all pointing to religious tolerance.

**Why it is asked:** The "coins with many deities = tolerance" argument and the Mahayana spread are frequent. Define once: *pluralistic* = made of many groups/faiths living together; *Vaishnavism* = devotion to Vishnu.

**The story (cause → effect):**
- **Cause:** the empire joined many peoples and faiths.
- **Effect:** **Mahayana Buddhism** flourished under Kanishka and spread to **China and Central Asia**; rulers like **Vima Kadphises** worshipped **Shiva** and some Kushanas supported **Vaishnavism**; coins showed **multiple deities**, and **stupas and temples for different faiths** were built.

**Picture it:**

| Strand | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Buddhism | Kanishka's patronage; Mahayana spread abroad |
| Shaivism | Vima Kadphises, Shiva/Nandi on coins |
| Vaishnavism | Support among some Kushanas |
| Tolerance | Multi-deity coins; shrines for many faiths |

**Terms explained:** *stupa* = a dome-shaped Buddhist shrine; *monastery* = a residence for monks.

**Don't confuse:** Kushana kings were **Buddhist patrons** *and* **Shiva devotees** at the same time — their tolerance is not a contradiction.

**Remember it:** "**Buddha + Shiva + Vishnu on the coins = tolerance.**"

**TL;DR**
- Mahayana Buddhism flourished under Kanishka and spread to China & Central Asia.
- Vima Kadphises and others worshipped Shiva; some supported Vaishnavism.
- Coins showed multiple deities — a pluralistic society.
- Stupas and temples for different faiths were built.
keyPoints: Mahayana Buddhism flourished under Kanishka and spread to China & Central Asia.
Vima Kadphises and others were devotees of Shiva; some supported Vaishnavism.
Coins depicted multiple deities — evidence of a pluralistic society.
Stupas and temples for different faiths were built across the empire.
items.mnemonic: Kushana faith mix — 'Buddha + Shiva + Vishnu on the coins' = tolerance.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Religion and Society under the Kushanas)

items.title: Decline & Legacy of the Kushanas
items.body:
## Decline & Legacy of the Kushanas

**In one line:** Kushana power faded after Vasudeva I, broken by the Sassanians in Central Asia and fragmentation in India, but their cultural legacy long outlived them.

**Why it is asked:** The *who ended them* (Sassanians) and the *last great ruler* (Vasudeva I) are standard, often in assertion-reason form. Define once: *Sassanians* = a powerful Persian/Iranian empire; *fragment* = to break into smaller pieces.

**The story (cause → event → result):**
- **Cause:** external pressure and over-stretch weakened the empire.
- **Event:** **Vasudeva I (early 3rd century CE)**, the last significant ruler, could not hold it; the **Sassanians overthrew the Kushanas in Central Asia** while Indian lands **split into smaller kingdoms**.
- **Result:** political power ended, but the Kushana **legacy survived** — the satrap system, the **Gandhara and Mathura art schools**, and **Mahayana Buddhism** — shaping later Indian dynasties.

**Terms explained:** *legacy* = what a group leaves behind for later ages; *satrap system* = rule through provincial governors.

**Don't confuse:** it was the **Sassanians** (Persia), not the Guptas, who overthrew the Kushanas in Central Asia; the Guptas rose later in India.

**Remember it:** "**Vasudeva last; Sassanians take Central Asia; India fragments — but the art and Mahayana live on.**"

**TL;DR**
- Vasudeva I (early 3rd century CE) was the last significant Kushana ruler.
- The Sassanians overthrew the Kushanas in Central Asia.
- Indian territories fragmented into smaller kingdoms.
- Legacy endured in art, religion and governance; influenced later dynasties.
keyPoints: Vasudeva I (early 3rd century CE) was the last significant Kushana ruler.
The Sassanians overthrew the Kushanas in Central Asia.
Indian territories fragmented into smaller kingdoms.
Legacy endured in art, religion and governance (satraps, Gandhara/Mathura art, Mahayana).
Influenced subsequent Indian dynasties.
items.mnemonic: Fall — 'Vasudeva last; Sassanians take Central Asia; India fragments'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Kushanas (Decline of the Kushana Empire)

items.title: Precision Facts the PYQs Hinge On (Council venue, Nagarjuna, Rajatarangini)
items.body:
## Precision Facts the PYQs Hinge On (Council venue, Nagarjuna, Rajatarangini)

**In one line:** A compact set of exact facts — the Fourth Council's venue and officers, the easily-forgotten Nagarjuna, and the sources that place Kanishka in Kashmir — that the exam keeps testing.

**Why it is asked:** These fine details decide close options. 

**Terms explained:** *Kundalavana* = the Kashmir site (near Srinagar) of the Fourth Council; *Mahavibhasha* = the great commentary compiled there; *Rajatarangini* = Kalhana's 12th-century chronicle of Kashmir; *Rabatak inscription* = a Kushana inscription in Afghanistan giving the royal genealogy.

### Fourth Buddhist Council — the exact details
- **Venue:** **Kundalavana (Kundalvana Vihara), near Srinagar in Kashmir** (some traditions place it at Jalandhar).
- **President:** **Vasumitra**; **Deputy:** **Ashvaghosha**.
- It compiled the commentary **Mahavibhasha** and finalised the **Mahayana–Hinayana** division; proceedings were in **Sanskrit** (not Pali).

### Court scholars — don't forget Nagarjuna
| Scholar | Known for |
|---|---|
| Ashvaghosha | Buddhacharita, Saundarananda |
| Charaka | Charaka Samhita — "father of Ayurveda" |
| Nagarjuna | Madhyamika / Sunyavada (Doctrine of the Void) |
| Vatsyayana | Kamasutra |

### Kanishka in the sources
- **Kalhana's Rajatarangini** records Kanishka's rule/invasion in **Kashmir**.
- Kanishka's **coins and inscriptions** are found at **Mathura, Sravasti, Kausambi and Sarnath (Benares)** — showing reach into the Ganga valley.
- The **Rabatak inscription** lists the genealogy **Kujula → Vima Takto → Vima Kadphises → Kanishka**.

**Don't confuse:** proceedings were in **Sanskrit** (Mahayana turn), *not* Pali; and the Fourth Council's president was **Vasumitra**, not Nagasena.

**Remember it:** "**Kundalavana + Vasumitra + Mahavibhasha; Rajatarangini remembers Kanishka.**"

**TL;DR**
- Fourth Council: Kundalavana (near Srinagar); President Vasumitra, Deputy Ashvaghosha; Mahavibhasha in Sanskrit.
- Nagarjuna (Sunyavada) was a leading Mahayana philosopher of the age.
- Kalhana's Rajatarangini records Kanishka in Kashmir.
- Coins/inscriptions at Mathura, Sravasti, Kausambi, Sarnath; Rabatak gives the genealogy.
keyPoints: Fourth Buddhist Council venue = Kundalavana (near Srinagar), Kashmir; President Vasumitra, Deputy Ashvaghosha; compiled the Mahavibhasha in Sanskrit.
Nagarjuna (Madhyamika/Sunyavada — Doctrine of the Void) was a leading Mahayana philosopher of the Kushana age.
Kalhana's Rajatarangini records Kanishka's rule/invasion in Kashmir.
Kanishka's coins/inscriptions found at Mathura, Sravasti, Kausambi and Sarnath (Benares).
The Rabatak inscription (Afghanistan) gives the Kushana genealogy up to Kanishka.
items.source: Kalhana's Rajatarangini; standard NCERT/ASI facts on the Fourth Buddhist Council (Kundalavana), Nagarjuna and the Rabatak inscription

items.title: For Mains — The Kushanas (Kanishka, art and the Silk Route)
items.body:
## For Mains — why the Kushanas matter

**Mains clause:** Paper-2 (History & Culture), clause **M2-1** — "Pre-history, IVC, Vedic, Mahajanapadas, Jainism/Buddhism, Magadha/Mauryas, Ashoka Dharma, **Kushans**" (`content/audit/syllabus-map.json`). The Kushanas are named explicitly in this clause.

Prelims tests *facts*; Mains asks you to argue the Kushana age as a peak of **political integration, cultural synthesis and trans-regional trade**. Build answers along these dimensions:

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Political reach | Empire from Central Asia to the Ganges valley; twin capitals Purushapura & Mathura; Devputra ideology |
| Administration | Satrapies under Mahakshatrapas; district/village officers; dual hereditary rule |
| Economy | Silk Route control; Indo-Roman trade; tri-metallic Roman-standard coinage |
| Religion | Mahayana Buddhism and the Fourth Council; Shaiva/Vaishnava devotion; tolerance |
| Art & learning | Gandhara and Mathura schools; Ashvaghosha, Charaka, Nagarjuna, Vatsyayana |
| Significance / limits | Bridge of civilisations; yet short-lived, overthrown by the Sassanians |

**Data points / sources to quote:** (1) **Saka era, 78 CE** — Kanishka's accession, India's national calendar; (2) **Fourth Buddhist Council** at **Kundalavana** under **Vasumitra**, compiling the **Mahavibhasha**; (3) **Gandhara (grey schist, Hellenistic)** vs **Mathura (red sandstone, indigenous)** art; (4) **Rabatak inscription** giving the royal genealogy; (5) **Kalhana's Rajatarangini** placing Kanishka in Kashmir.

**AP angle:** the **Amravati school** of the lower Krishna valley (Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda in Andhra Pradesh), under the **Satavahanas and Ikshvakus**, is the perfect contrast to the Kushana-patronised Gandhara/Mathura schools — letting you tie the northern Kushana art story to Andhra's own marble-relief tradition and the philosopher **Nagarjuna** (linked to Nagarjunakonda).

**Use in answers:**
- *Example:* use the multi-deity coins to argue that Kushana kingship rested on religious tolerance.
- *Quote idea:* describe Gandhara as "Indian in subject, Graeco-Roman in form".
- *Diagram idea:* a map of the Silk Route marking Purushapura, Mathura and the Indo-Roman trade flows.
